title: "Learning Rate Scheduler"
description: "A training strategy that changes the learning rate according to a schedule or training signal."
term: "Learning Rate Scheduler"
letter: "L"

difficulty: "Intermediate"

## Simple explanation

A learning-rate scheduler changes how large the model's training steps are as
training progresses. It may start cautiously, reduce the rate over time, or
adjust it when progress stalls.

## Technical explanation

A scheduler defines a sequence of learning rates $\eta_t$ for optimizer steps
or epochs. Common schedules include step decay, exponential decay, cosine
decay, and warmup followed by decay. Some schedulers respond to a measured
signal, such as a validation metric, rather than a fixed timeline.

The optimizer applies updates using the current learning rate; the scheduler
does not replace the optimizer or compute gradients itself.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

One constant learning rate may not be ideal throughout training. A schedule
can support stable early optimization and smaller later updates, and can be
important when reproducing a model's training recipe.

## How it works

The training loop calls a scheduler at the intended interval, updating the
optimizer's learning rate according to its rule. A cosine schedule, for
example, gradually reduces a starting rate over a chosen duration. The
schedule's step timing must match the framework's expected convention.

## Practical example

An LLM fine-tuning run may warm up the learning rate over the first few
hundred optimizer steps, then decay it toward the end. Warmup can reduce the
risk of large early updates, while decay can help training settle.

## Common misconceptions

- A scheduler does not automatically improve every training run; its shape and timing depend on the task.
- A scheduler's progress counter may advance per batch, optimizer step, or epoch, depending on its design.
- Learning-rate scheduling is not the same as changing batch size.
